what_it_does: A processor's front end is the part that fetches the next instructions to execute before it knows what they do. Server programs are huge — the collection of machine-code instructions they use (the 'instruction working set') is so large that it does not all fit in the small, fast instruction cache on the chip, causing the processor to stall while it fetches needed instructions from slower memory. Existing prefetchers try to replay an exact recorded sequence of instruction addresses, but real server traffic takes slightly different paths through the code each time, making those recordings go stale. Hierarchical Prefetching solves this by working at a coarser level. A one-time software analysis of the server binary groups related code into larger regions called Bundles — chunks spanning tens to hundreds of kilobytes that tend to execute together for a given type of request. When the processor detects it is about to enter a Bundle, it fetches the whole Bundle into the instruction cache early, tolerating the inevitable small variations in which exact lines are executed. Only a tiny amount of on-chip storage (under 2 kilobytes of fast static memory) is needed for the bundle-detection logic, while the detailed bundle descriptions live in main memory and are brought in on demand.
